title: Τὰ ὅπλα καὶ Μελανθώ
titleEn: The Arms Put Away and Melantho’s Taunt — Odyssey 19.1–103
part: The Arms Put Away and Melantho’s Taunt (19.1–103)
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: With the suitors asleep, Odysseus tells Telemachus to carry the arms out of the hall, and to put the suitors off with an excuse about smoke and the danger of drink. Telemachus has his nurse Eurycleia shut the women away, and father and son carry the helmets, shields and spears inside while Athena lights their work with a golden lamp. Telemachus is struck by the glow on the walls; Odysseus tells him to say nothing and go to bed, and stays behind to stir the household. Penelope comes down and sits by the fire, the maids clear the tables and pile fresh logs on the braziers, and Melantho abuses the stranger a second time. Odysseus answers her sharply, and Penelope, overhearing, rebukes Melantho and orders a seat for the stranger, so that she may question him. She begins to speak as he sits down.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ ἐν μεγάρῳ ὑπελείπετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
μνηστήρεσσι φόνον σὺν Ἀθήνῃ μερμηρίζων·
sentences.tr:
autar ho en megarōi hypeleipeto dios Odysseus,
mnēstēressi phonon syn Athēnēi mermērizōn·
sentences.l:
But he in the hall was left behind, heavenly Odysseus,
for the suitors slaughter with Athena pondering.
sentences.i: But heavenly Odysseus was left behind in the hall, pondering slaughter for the suitors with Athena.
sentences.n: Book 19 takes up Odysseus at once, alone in the hall while the suitors sleep, with the household armour still on the walls. ὑπελείπετο is the imperfect passive of ὑπολείπω ‘leave behind’, ‘was left behind’; he stays on purpose, and at line 44 he announces ὑπολείψομαι αὐτοῦ ‘I will stay behind here’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is his stock epithet, translated every time. μνηστήρεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι, ‘for the suitors’, and φόνον is ‘slaughter’. μερμηρίζων ‘pondering’ is from μερμηρίζω ‘be in doubt, turn over in the mind’. σὺν Ἀθήνῃ ‘with Athena’ makes the goddess his partner in the plan. Line 1 is also 7.230, where it describes him left in the hall of Alcinous.

sentences.t: αἶψα δὲ Τηλέμαχον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: aipsa de Tēlemachon epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: And at once, to Telemachus, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he spoke winged words to Telemachus:
sentences.n: ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘he spoke winged words’: πτερόεντα ‘winged’ pictures words as flying from speaker to hearer, and it is translated every time. προσηύδα is the unaugmented imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. αἶψα is ‘at once’. The ano teleia at the end marks the speech that follows.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχε, χρὴ τεύχε’ ἀρήϊα κατθέμεν εἴσω
πάντα μάλ’·
sentences.tr:
Tēlemache, chrē teuche’ arēïa katthemen eisō
panta mal’·
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, it is needful the warlike armour to lay away within,
all of it, every bit;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, you must put away the warlike armour inside, all of it, every piece;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. Odysseus gives his son the order he gave him at 16.284–285, nearly in the same words; the end of line 5 and line 6 are 16.286–287, and the excuse that follows is the one at 16.288–294: the arms must be taken out of the hall. χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes an infinitive, and κατθέμεν is καταθέμεναι ‘to lay away’, an Epic infinitive in -μεν. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour, gear’ with its last vowel elided, and ἀρήϊα ‘warlike’ goes with it. εἴσω is ‘inside’. πάντα μάλ’ is ‘all, every bit’, with μάλα strengthening πάντα.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ μνηστῆρας μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσι
παρφάσθαι, ὅτε κέν σε μεταλλῶσιν ποθέοντες·
sentences.tr:
autar mnēstēras malakois epeessi
parphasthai, hote ken se metallōsin potheontes·
sentences.l:
and the suitors with soft words
to put off, when they question you, missing them:
sentences.i: and put off the suitors with soft words whenever, missing the armour, they question you:
sentences.n: παρφάσθαι is the middle infinitive of παράφημι ‘talk round, put off’, standing as an order. μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσι is ‘with soft words’, a dative plural in -εσσι. ὅτε κέν with the subjunctive μεταλλῶσιν is ‘whenever they inquire’, from μεταλλάω ‘ask’. ποθέοντες ‘missing, longing for’ has no object in the Greek; the armour is understood, as the answer in the next lines shows. The colon introduces the excuse that Telemachus is to give.

sentences.t:
ἐκ καπνοῦ κατέθηκ’, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι τοῖσιν ἐῴκει
οἷά ποτε Τροίηνδε κιὼν κατέλειπεν Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἀλλὰ κατῄκισται, ὅσσον πυρὸς ἵκετ’ ἀϋτμή.
sentences.tr:
ek kapnou katethēk’, epei ouketi toisin eōikei
hoia pote Troiēnde kiōn kateleipen Odysseus,
alla katēikistai, hosson pyros hiket’ aÿtmē.
sentences.l:
‘Out of the smoke I have put them away, since no longer like those
were they that once, to Troy going, Odysseus left,
but they have been marred, as far as the blast of fire reached.
sentences.i: ‘I have put them away out of the smoke, since they are no longer like those that Odysseus left behind when he went to Troy, but have been marred as far as the breath of the fire has reached.
sentences.n: These lines are the excuse Odysseus tells Telemachus to give the suitors, so this is a speech inside a speech, marked in the English with single quotes. Telemachus is the speaker inside the quotation, which is why Odysseus is spoken of in the third person. The quotation runs to the end of line 13. κατέθηκ’ is κατέθηκα ‘I put away’, the aorist of κατατίθημι. ἐῴκει is the pluperfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative τοῖσιν ‘to those’. οἷα ποτε is ‘such as once’, Τροίηνδε has the suffix -δε ‘to Troy’, and κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’. κατῄκισται is the perfect passive of καταικίζω ‘disfigure, mar’. ὅσσον is ‘as far as’, and ἀϋτμή is ‘breath, blast’.

sentences.t:
πρὸς δ’ ἔτι καὶ τόδε μεῖζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ἔμβαλε δαίμων
μή πως οἰνωθέντες, ἔριν στήσαντες ἐν ὑμῖν,
ἀλλήλους τρώσητε καταισχύνητέ τε δαῖτα
καὶ μνηστύν· αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος.
sentences.tr:
pros d’ eti kai tode meizon eni phresin embale daimōn
mē pōs oinōthentes, erin stēsantes en hymin,
allēlous trōsēte kataischynēte te daita
kai mnēstyn· autos gar ephelketai andra sidēros.
sentences.l:
And besides this, the greater thing too into my mind a power put,
lest somehow, having been made drunk, having set up strife among you,
each other you wound and shame the feast
and the wooing; for of itself draws to it a man iron.’”
sentences.i: And besides, some power has put this greater thought into my mind, for fear that, grown drunk and having stirred up strife among you, you may wound one another and disgrace the feast and the wooing; for iron of itself draws a man toward it.’”
sentences.n: This is the second reason Telemachus is to give, and it closes both the quotation and Odysseus’ speech, which is why the unit runs on past the stop after μνηστύν to the end of line 13. πρὸς δ’ ἔτι καί is ‘and furthermore’, and τόδε μεῖζον ‘this greater thing’ prepares the μή clause. δαίμων is ‘some power’, a divine force left unnamed; at 16.291 the same lines have Κρονίων ‘the son of Cronus’ in its place. μή πως with the subjunctives τρώσητε and καταισχύνητε is a fear, ‘lest somehow you wound and disgrace’. οἰνωθέντες is the aorist passive participle of οἰνόω ‘make drunk’. αὐτός means ‘of itself’, and ἐφέλκεται is ‘draws to itself’: a saying that iron at hand leads men to use it. σίδηρος ‘iron’ stands for weapons.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθετο πατρί,
ἐκ δὲ καλεσσάμενος προσέφη τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Tēlemachos de philōi epepeitheto patri,
ek de kalessamenos prosephē trophon Eurykleian·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and, calling her out, addressed the nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father; he called the nurse Eurycleia out and said to her:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here, and ὣς φάτο ‘So he spoke’ closes Odysseus’ speech. ἐπεπείθετο is from πείθομαι ‘obey’, which takes the dative, here φίλῳ πατρί ‘his dear father’. ἐκ … καλεσσάμενος is a tmesis of ἐκκαλέομαι ‘call out’, with the double σ of the Epic aorist. προσέφη is ‘addressed’. τροφός is the ‘nurse’ who brought him up, and Εὐρύκλειαν is the accusative of her name.

sentences.t:
μαῖ’, ἄγε δή μοι ἔρυξον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναῖκας,
ὄφρα κεν ἐς θάλαμον καταθείομαι ἔντεα πατρὸς
καλά, τά μοι κατὰ οἶκον ἀκηδέα καπνὸς ἀμέρδει
πατρὸς ἀποιχομένοιο·
sentences.tr:
mai’, age dē moi eryxon eni megaroisi gynaikas,
ophra ken es thalamon katatheiomai entea patros
kala, ta moi kata oikon akēdea kapnos amerdei
patros apoichomenoio·
sentences.l:
“Nurse, come now, for me hold back in the halls the women,
so that into a chamber I may put away my father’s armour,
the fine, which for me throughout the house, uncared-for, the smoke robs,
my father being gone away;
sentences.i: “Nurse, come now, keep the women back in the halls for me, so that I may put away in a chamber the fine armour of my father, which the smoke in the house has been spoiling, neglected as it is, while my father is gone away;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. Telemachus asks the nurse to keep the women away while he stores the armour; to her he gives the same reason he was told to give the suitors, the smoke. μαῖα is a respectful address to an older woman, ‘Nurse’ here. ἔρυξον is the aorist imperative of ἐρύκω ‘hold back, keep in’. καταθείομαι is the aorist subjunctive middle of κατατίθημι, with a lengthened vowel, ‘that I may put away’, after ὄφρα κεν. ἔντεα is ‘gear’, the armour. ἀκηδέα is ‘uncared-for’ (ἀ- + κῆδος ‘care’). ἀμέρδει is from ἀμέρδω ‘rob, deprive’, and what it takes from the armour is left unsaid; the sense is that the smoke spoils it. πατρὸς ἀποιχομένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘my father being gone’.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δ’ ἔτι νήπιος ἦα.
sentences.tr: egō d’ eti nēpios ēa.
sentences.l: and I still an infant was.
sentences.i: and I was still an infant.
sentences.n: ἦα is the Ionic first-person imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). νήπιος is ‘infant’, a word built on ἀ- + ἔπος and meaning literally ‘without speech’: Telemachus was a baby when his father sailed for Troy, so he had no hand in the armour’s neglect.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἐθέλω καταθέσθαι, ἵν’ οὐ πυρὸς ἵξετ’ ἀϋτμή.
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ethelō katathesthai, hin’ ou pyros hixet’ aÿtmē.
sentences.l: But now I wish to put them away, where of fire the blast will not come.”
sentences.i: But now I want to put them away, where the breath of the fire will not reach them.”
sentences.n: καταθέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of κατατίθημι, ‘to put away for myself’, as καταθείομαι at line 17. ἵνα here means ‘where’, with the future ἵξετ’, the elided ἵξεται of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach, come to’. ἀϋτμή is ‘breath, blast’; the same phrase stands in the excuse at line 9. Telemachus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the formula for a reply: αὖτε ‘in turn, again’ marks that the speaker has changed, and προσέειπε is ‘addressed’. φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια ‘the dear nurse Eurycleia’ is her stock name-phrase, φίλη ‘dear’ translated every time. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ δή ποτε, τέκνον, ἐπιφροσύνας ἀνέλοιο
οἴκου κήδεσθαι καὶ κτήματα πάντα φυλάσσειν.
sentences.tr:
ai gar dē pote, teknon, epiphrosynas aneloio
oikou kēdesthai kai ktēmata panta phylassein.
sentences.l:
“Would that indeed, once, child, presence of mind you would take up
to care for the house and to guard all the possessions.
sentences.i: “If only, my child, you would at last take up some presence of mind, to care for the house and guard all its possessions.
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ opens a wish, ‘would that, if only’, and δή ποτε is ‘at last, some time’. ἐπιφροσύνας is the plural of ἐπιφροσύνη ‘presence of mind’, the word Athena gives Odysseus at 5.437, and here it means the habit of thinking ahead. ἀνέλοιο is the aorist optative middle of ἀναιρέομαι ‘take up’. τέκνον is ‘child’. κήδεσθαι is the infinitive of κήδομαι ‘care for’, with the genitive οἴκου ‘the house’. κτήματα ‘possessions’ is the object of φυλάσσειν ‘to guard’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε, τίς τοι ἔπειτα μετοιχομένη φάος οἴσει;
sentences.tr: all’ age, tis toi epeita metoichomenē phaos oisei;
sentences.l: But come, who for you then, going along, a light will carry?
sentences.i: But come, who is to go with you and carry the light?
sentences.n: τίς … οἴσει is ‘who will carry’, the future of φέρω. μετοιχομένη is the feminine participle of μετοίχομαι ‘go after, go along with’, and its feminine form shows that Eurycleia means a woman, one of the maids. φάος is ‘light’, a lamp or torch, and τοι is ‘for you’, the enclitic dative. Eurycleia’s point is that, with the maids kept back, nobody is left to carry a light.

sentences.t: δμῳὰς δ’ οὐκ εἴας προβλωσκέμεν, αἵ κεν ἔφαινον.
sentences.tr: dmōias d’ ouk eias problōskemen, hai ken ephainon.
sentences.l: But the maidservants you did not allow to go forth, who would have given light.”
sentences.i: But you would not let the maids come forward, who would have given light.”
sentences.n: δμῳάς is ‘maidservants’. εἴας is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, and προβλωσκέμεν is the infinitive of προβλώσκω ‘go forward’, an Epic infinitive in -έμεν. αἵ κεν ἔφαινον is a relative clause with κεν and the imperfect, ‘who would have given light’, the light they would have given if allowed. Eurycleia’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα is the formula by which Telemachus replies: αὖ ‘in turn’, ἀντίον ‘face to face’, and πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is his stock epithet, translated every time. ηὔδα is the unaugmented imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: ξεῖνος ὅδ’·
sentences.tr: xeinos hod’·
sentences.l: “This stranger here;
sentences.i: “It will be this stranger;
sentences.n: ξεῖνος ὅδ’ has no verb: Telemachus answers Eurycleia’s question ‘who will carry the light?’ with ‘this stranger’, and the verb is understood from her words. ὅδ’ is ὅδε ‘this here’, elided. The stop printed after it makes the next words a separate unit.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἀεργὸν ἀνέξομαι ὅς κεν ἐμῆς γε
χοίνικος ἅπτηται, καὶ τηλόθεν εἰληλουθώς.
sentences.tr:
ou gar aergon anexomai hos ken emēs ge
choinikos haptētai, kai tēlothen eilēlouthōs.
sentences.l:
for an idle man I will not tolerate, whoever my own, at least,
measure may touch, even one from far away come.”
sentences.i: for I will not put up with anyone idle who lays a hand on my measure of grain, even one who has come from far away.”
sentences.n: οὐ … ἀνέξομαι is ‘I will not put up with’, the future of ἀνέχομαι. ἀεργός ‘idle’ is ἀ- + ἔργον ‘work’. ὅς κεν … ἅπτηται is a general clause, ‘whoever touches’, with the subjunctive. A χοῖνιξ is a dry measure of about a quart, a man’s daily ration of grain, so touching it means eating from Telemachus’ stores, and ἐμῆς γε stresses that it is his own. καὶ τηλόθεν εἰληλουθώς is ‘even one who has come from far away’: καί with a participle is concessive, and εἰληλουθώς is the perfect participle of ἔρχομαι. Telemachus speaks as a master who feeds no idlers, and so sets the stranger to work.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος.
sentences.tr: hōs ar’ ephōnēsen, tēi d’ apteros epleto mythos.
sentences.l: So then he spoke, and to her wingless was the speech.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and for her the speech was wingless.
sentences.n: ἄπτερος ‘wingless’ is the opposite of the formula ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’: the speech did not fly to its hearer. It is usually taken to mean that Eurycleia made no reply, but the Greek does not say so. The same line stands at 17.57, of Penelope. τῇ is ‘for her’, the dative of the person concerned, and ἔπλετο is the aorist of πέλομαι ‘become, be’, which carries the ordinary augment ἐ-. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: κλήϊσεν δὲ θύρας μεγάρων εὖ ναιεταόντων.
sentences.tr: klēïsen de thyras megarōn eu naietaontōn.
sentences.l: And she shut the doors of the well-inhabited halls.
sentences.i: She shut the doors of the well-inhabited halls.
sentences.n: Eurycleia does what Telemachus asked and shuts the doors. κλήϊσεν is the aorist of κλῄω ‘shut’ in its Ionic form. εὖ ναιεταόντων ‘well-inhabited’ is the genitive plural of a participle of ναιετάω ‘dwell, be inhabited’, and it is the stock epithet for a house that is full of life.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἄρ’ ἀναΐξαντ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ φαίδιμος υἱὸς
ἐσφόρεον κόρυθάς τε καὶ ἀσπίδας ὀμφαλοέσσας
ἔγχεά τ’ ὀξυόεντα·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ ar’ anaïxant’ Odyseus kai phaidimos huios
esphoreon korythas te kai aspidas omphaloessas
enchea t’ oxyoenta·
sentences.i: The two of them, Odysseus and his glorious son, sprang up and began carrying in the helmets and the shields with bosses and the sharp spears;
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual ‘the two’, Odysseus and his son, and ἀναΐξαντ’ is the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. ἐσφόρεον is the imperfect of εἰσφορέω ‘carry in’, ‘they set about carrying in’. κόρυς is a ‘helmet’, and ὀμφαλοέσσας agrees with ἀσπίδας: ὀμφαλός is ‘navel’ and also the ‘boss’ of a shield, so ‘shields with bosses’. ὀξυόεντα is ‘sharp’, built on ὀξύς, and ἔγχεα are ‘spears’.

sentences.t:
πάροιθε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη,
χρύσεον λύχνον ἔχουσα, φάος περικαλλὲς ἐποίει.
sentences.tr:
paroithe de Pallas Athēnē,
chryseon lychnon echousa, phaos perikalles epoiei.
sentences.l:
and in front Pallas Athena,
holding a golden lamp, was making a very fair light.
sentences.i: and in front of them Pallas Athena, holding a golden lamp, was making a very fair light.
sentences.n: Athena herself lights the work, which is why the hall seems to glow in Telemachus’ next speech. πάροιθε is ‘in front’. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is ‘Pallas Athena’; the meaning of Παλλάς is disputed. χρύσεον λύχνον is ‘a golden lamp’, ἔχουσα ‘holding’. ἐποίει is the imperfect, ‘was making’, and περικαλλές ‘very fair’ goes with φάος ‘light’.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε Τηλέμαχος προσεφώνεεν ὃν πατέρ’ αἶψα·
sentences.tr: dē tote Tēlemachos prosephōneen hon pater’ aipsa·
sentences.l: Then indeed Telemachus spoke to his own father at once:
sentences.i: Then Telemachus at once spoke to his own father:
sentences.n: δὴ τότε … ‘then indeed …’ introduces a speech that is not a reply. προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’, and ὃν πατέρ’ is ‘his own father’, with the possessive ὅς ‘his own’ (not the relative). αἶψα is ‘at once’.

sentences.t: ὦ πάτερ, ἦ μέγα θαῦμα τόδ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῶμαι.
sentences.tr: ō pater, ē mega thauma tod’ ophthalmoisin horōmai.
sentences.l: “O father, truly a great wonder this with my eyes I see.
sentences.i: “Father, this is truly a great wonder that I see with my eyes.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. Telemachus has seen the glow Athena makes. ἦ is ‘truly’, θαῦμα ‘a wonder’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, ‘with my eyes’. ὁρῶμαι is the middle form of ὁρῶ ‘see’, with no difference in sense.

sentences.t:
ἔμπης μοι τοῖχοι μεγάρων καλαί τε μεσόδμαι,
εἰλάτιναί τε δοκοί, καὶ κίονες ὑψόσ’ ἔχοντες
φαίνοντ’ ὀφθαλμοῖς ὡς εἰ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο.
sentences.tr:
empēs moi toichoi megarōn kalai te mesodmai,
eilatinai te dokoi, kai kiones hypsos’ echontes
phainont’ ophthalmois hōs ei pyros aithomenoio.
sentences.l:
All the same, to me the walls of the hall and the fine cross-timbers,
and the fir beams, and the pillars holding up on high,
appear to the eyes as if of fire burning.
sentences.i: All the same, to my eyes the walls of the hall and the fine cross-timbers, and the fir beams, and the pillars that hold it up on high, appear as though of burning fire.
sentences.n: ἔμπης is ‘all the same, in any case’: whatever the cause, so it looks. The subject is a long list, τοῖχοι ‘walls’, μεσόδμαι, δοκοί ‘beams’ and κίονες ‘pillars’, with φαίνοντ’ (φαίνονται ‘appear’) held back to the third line. μεσόδμη is the mast-block in a ship, and in a house it is some part of the framing; the exact fitting is not known, and ‘cross-timbers’ is a guess. εἰλάτιναι is ‘of fir’. ὑψόσ’ is ὑψόσε ‘up on high’, with ἔχοντες ‘holding’. ὡς εἰ is ‘as if’, and αἰθομένοιο ‘burning’ is the participle of αἴθομαι.

sentences.t: ἦ μάλα τις θεὸς ἔνδον, οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι.
sentences.tr: ē mala tis theos endon, hoi ouranon euryn echousi.
sentences.l: Truly indeed some god is within, of those who hold the wide heaven.”
sentences.i: Surely some god is in here, one of those who hold the wide heaven.”
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα is ‘truly, indeed’, and ἔνδον ‘inside’. οἳ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι ‘who hold the wide heaven’ is a plural relative clause after the singular τις θεός: some god among the gods who hold the sky as their domain. Telemachus is right, as the reader knows from line 33. His speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is the formula ‘answering him addressed’: ἀπαμείβομαι is ‘answer’, and the participle with προσέφη gives ‘in answer … said to him’. πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is Odysseus’ stock epithet, translated every time; μῆτις is cunning intelligence, craft. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: σίγα καὶ κατὰ σὸν νόον ἴσχανε μηδ’ ἐρέεινε·
sentences.tr: siga kai kata son noon ischane mēd’ ereeine·
sentences.l: “Be silent, and in your own mind hold it back, and do not question;
sentences.i: “Be silent, keep it to yourself in your own mind, and ask no questions;
sentences.n: σίγα is the imperative of σιγάω ‘be silent’. κατὰ σὸν νόον ἴσχανε is ‘hold it back in your own mind’: ἴσχανε is the imperative of ἰσχάνω ‘hold back, restrain’. μηδ’ ἐρέεινε is ‘and do not question’, the imperative of ἐρεείνω ‘ask’. Telemachus is not to ask what the glow is.

sentences.t: αὕτη τοι δίκη ἐστὶ θεῶν, οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν.
sentences.tr: hautē toi dikē esti theōn, hoi Olympon echousin.
sentences.l: This, you know, is the way of the gods, who hold Olympus.
sentences.i: That is the way of the gods who hold Olympus.
sentences.n: δίκη is ‘way, custom’, what is usual for the gods. τοι is ‘you know’, and αὕτη ‘this’ points to the wonder. οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν ‘who hold Olympus’ is a relative clause. Odysseus does not name Athena: he says only that such things are what gods do, and are not to be asked about.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν κατάλεξαι, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑπολείψομαι αὐτοῦ,
ὄφρα κ’ ἔτι δμῳὰς καὶ μητέρα σὴν ἐρεθίζω·
sentences.tr:
alla sy men katalexai, egō d’ hypoleipsomai autou,
ophra k’ eti dmōias kai mētera sēn erethizō·
sentences.l:
But you go and lie down, and I will stay behind here,
so that I may still further provoke the maidservants and your mother;
sentences.i: But you go and lie down, and I will stay behind here, so that I may stir up the maids and your mother still further;
sentences.n: κατάλεξαι is the aorist imperative middle of καταλέγω ‘lay oneself down’. ὑπολείψομαι is the future middle of ὑπολείπω ‘stay behind’, the verb of ὑπελείπετο in line 1, and αὐτοῦ is ‘right here’. ὄφρα κ’ … ἐρεθίζω is a purpose clause, κ’ being κε with the subjunctive; ἐρεθίζω is ‘provoke, stir up’, and ἔτι ‘still further’. δμῳάς are ‘maidservants’. Odysseus says openly what he means to do: set the women stirring so that Penelope will question him.

sentences.t: ἡ δέ μ’ ὀδυρομένη εἰρήσεται ἀμφὶς ἕκαστα.
sentences.tr: hē de m’ odyromenē eirēsetai amphis hekasta.
sentences.l: and she, lamenting, will ask me each thing separately.”
sentences.i: and she, lamenting, will ask me about each thing separately.”
sentences.n: ἡ δέ is ‘and she’, Penelope. ὀδυρομένη is ‘lamenting’. εἰρήσεται is the future of εἴρομαι ‘ask’ (Attic ἐρήσεται), with the accusative μέ ‘me’ and ἕκαστα ‘each thing’. ἀμφίς is ‘apart, separately’, so ἀμφὶς ἕκαστα is ‘each thing by itself’. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
κείων ἐς θάλαμον, δαΐδων ὕπο λαμπομενάων,
ἔνθα πάρος κοιμᾶθ’, ὅτε μιν γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἱκάνοι·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, Tēlemachos de diek megaroio bebēkei
keiōn es thalamon, daïdōn hypo lampomenaōn,
entha paros koimath’, hote min glykys hypnos hikanoi·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Telemachus went out through the hall to his chamber, wanting to lie down, under flaring torches, to the place where he used to sleep whenever sweet sleep came upon him;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. ὣς φάτο ‘So he spoke’ closes Odysseus’ speech. διὲκ is ‘out through’, διά and ἐκ together, with the genitive μεγάροιο. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘he had gone’. κείων is the desiderative participle κείω, from κεῖμαι, ‘wishing to lie down’, as κείοντες at 18.428. δαΐδων ὕπο ‘under torches’ puts the preposition after its noun, and λαμπομενάων ‘shining, flaring’ is the genitive plural of the participle of λάμπω. ἔνθα is ‘where’, πάρος ‘formerly’, and κοιμᾶθ’ is the imperfect of κοιμάομαι, ‘used to sleep’; ὅτε μιν … ἱκάνοι is an optative of repeated action, ‘whenever sleep came upon him’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἄρα καὶ τότ’ ἔλεκτο καὶ Ἠῶ δῖαν ἔμιμνεν.
sentences.tr: enth’ ara kai tot’ elekto kai Ēō dian emimnen.
sentences.l: There then, even then, he lay down and waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.i: There he lay down on that night too, and waited for heavenly Dawn.
sentences.n: ἔλεκτο is the aorist middle of λέγω in its old sense ‘lay down’. ἔνθ’ ἄρα καὶ τότ’ is ‘there, then, even then’: as on other nights. Ἠῶ δῖαν ‘heavenly Dawn’ is a stock phrase, δῖα ‘heavenly’ translated every time. ἔμιμνεν is the imperfect of μίμνω ‘wait for’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ ἐν μεγάρῳ ὑπελείπετο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
μνηστήρεσσι φόνον σὺν Ἀθήνῃ μερμηρίζων.
sentences.tr:
autar ho en megarōi hypeleipeto dios Odysseus,
mnēstēressi phonon syn Athēnēi mermērizōn.
sentences.l:
But he in the hall was left behind, heavenly Odysseus,
for the suitors slaughter with Athena pondering.
sentences.i: But heavenly Odysseus was left behind in the hall, pondering slaughter for the suitors with Athena.
sentences.n: Lines 51–52 repeat lines 1–2, apart from the stop at the end. Telemachus is in bed, so the picture of Odysseus alone in the hall begins again: a ring that closes the first scene before Penelope enters.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἴεν ἐκ θαλάμοιο περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
Ἀρτέμιδι ἰκέλη ἠὲ χρυσέῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ien ek thalamoio periphrōn Pēnelopeia,
Artemidi ikelē ēe chryseēi Aphroditēi.
sentences.l:
And she came out of her chamber, circumspect Penelope,
like to Artemis or golden Aphrodite,
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope came out of her chamber, like Artemis or golden Aphrodite,
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here, and Penelope comes down. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, and ἴεν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘came’. θαλάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο, ‘out of her chamber’. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια ‘circumspect Penelope’ is her stock name-phrase, translated every time. ἰκέλη ‘like’ takes the dative, here Ἀρτέμιδι and Ἀφροδίτῃ, and χρυσέῃ ‘golden’ is Aphrodite’s epithet. The same two lines describe her at 17.36–37.

sentences.t:
τῇ παρὰ μὲν κλισίην πυρὶ κάτθεσαν, ἔνθ’ ἄρ’ ἐφῖζε,
δινωτὴν ἐλέφαντι καὶ ἀργύρῳ·
sentences.tr:
tēi para men klisiēn pyri katthesan, enth’ ar’ ephize,
dinōtēn elephanti kai argyrōi·
sentences.l:
and for her beside the fire a seat they set, where she then sat,
round-wrought, with ivory and silver;
sentences.i: and they set a seat for her beside the fire, where she then sat, worked in rounds with ivory and silver;
sentences.n: τῇ παρὰ … κάτθεσαν is a tmesis, κάτθεσαν standing for κατέθεσαν, ‘set beside’, with τῇ ‘for her’ and πυρί ‘by the fire’. κλισίη is a seat to lean back in, from the root of κλίνω; the same word is ‘hut’ at 14.194. ἐφῖζε is the imperfect of ἐφίζω ‘sit down upon’. δινωτήν is from δινέω ‘turn round’, and its exact sense is not certain: turned on a lathe, or inlaid in rings and curves. ἐλέφαντι καὶ ἀργύρῳ are datives of material, ‘with ivory and silver’.

sentences.t:
ἥν ποτε τέκτων
ποίησ’ Ἰκμάλιος, καὶ ὑπὸ θρῆνυν ποσὶν ἧκε
προσφυέ’ ἐξ αὐτῆς, ὅθ’ ἐπὶ μέγα βάλλετο κῶας.
sentences.tr:
hēn pote tektōn
poiēs’ Ikmalios, kai hypo thrēnyn posin hēke
prosphye’ ex autēs, hoth’ epi mega balleto kōas.
sentences.l:
which once the craftsman
Icmalius made, and under it for the feet a footstool he set,
attached to it, where a great fleece was thrown.
sentences.i: The craftsman Icmalius had once made it, and had set beneath it a footstool for the feet, joined to it, on which a great fleece was thrown.
sentences.n: ἥν is the relative ‘which’, the seat. ποίησ’ is ποίησε ‘made’, and τέκτων is ‘craftsman, carpenter’. Ἰκμάλιος is the maker’s name. ὑπὸ … ἧκε is a tmesis, ‘put under’, from ἵημι. θρῆνυν is ‘footstool’, and προσφυέ’ ἐξ αὐτῆς is ‘attached to it, of a piece with it’. ὅθ’ is ὅθι ‘where’, and ἐπὶ … βάλλετο is a tmesis, a middle in a passive sense, ‘was laid on’. κῶας is ‘fleece’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἔπειτα περίφρων Πηνελόπεια.
sentences.tr: entha kathezet’ epeita periphrōn Pēnelopeia.
sentences.l: There then sat down circumspect Penelope.
sentences.i: There circumspect Penelope sat down.
sentences.n: ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἔπειτα is the formula for taking a seat, ‘there sat down then’; it stands at 16.48 for Telemachus. καθέζετ’ is καθέζετο, the imperfect of καθέζομαι ‘sit down’. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια is her name-phrase again.

sentences.t: ἦλθον δὲ δμῳαὶ λευκώλενοι ἐκ μεγάροιο.
sentences.tr: ēlthon de dmōiai leukōlenoi ek megaroio.
sentences.l: And came the white-armed maidservants out of the hall.
sentences.i: The white-armed maids came out of the hall.
sentences.n: δμῳαί are ‘maidservants’, and λευκώλενοι ‘white-armed’ is their epithet here, translated every time. ἐκ μεγάροιο is ‘out of the hall’, a genitive in -οιο. ἦλθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι ‘came’.

sentences.t:
αἱ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν σῖτον πολὺν ᾕρεον ἠδὲ τραπέζας
καὶ δέπα, ἔνθεν ἄρ’ ἄνδρες ὑπερμενέοντες ἔπινον·
sentences.tr:
hai d’ apo men siton polyn hēireon ēde trapezas
kai depa, enthen ar’ andres hypermeneontes epinon·
sentences.l:
And they, much food, took away, and the tables
and the cups, from which the exceeding-strong men were drinking;
sentences.i: They took away the great quantity of food, and the tables and the cups from which the men of surpassing strength had been drinking;
sentences.n: ἀπὸ … ᾕρεον is a tmesis of ἀφαιρέω ‘take away’, with the object σῖτον πολύν ‘much food’. τραπέζας are ‘tables’ and δέπα is the plural of δέπας ‘cup’. ἔνθεν is ‘from which’. ὑπερμενέοντες is from ὑπερμενής ‘of surpassing strength’; of the suitors it carries a tone of arrogance, not praise. ἔπινον is the imperfect, ‘were drinking’.

sentences.t:
πῦρ δ’ ἀπὸ λαμπτήρων χαμάδις βάλον, ἄλλα δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῶν
νήησαν ξύλα πολλά, φόως ἔμεν ἠδὲ θέρεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
pyr d’ apo lamptērōn chamadis balon, alla d’ ep’ autōn
nēēsan xyla polla, phoōs emen ēde theresthai.
sentences.l:
and the fire from the braziers on the ground they threw, and others on them
they heaped, logs many, to be a light and to warm themselves.
sentences.i: and they threw the fire from the braziers on the ground, and heaped other logs on top of them, many of them, to give light and warmth.
sentences.n: πῦρ … ἀπὸ … βάλον is a tmesis of ἀποβάλλω, ‘threw off’, and χαμάδις is ‘to the ground’. λαμπτήρων ‘braziers’ are the ones set up at 18.307 to light the hall. νήησαν is the aorist of νηέω ‘heap up’, and ἐπ’ αὐτῶν is ‘on them’. φόως ἔμεν is ‘to be a light’, with the Epic φόως for φῶς and the infinitive ἔμεν for εἶναι. θέρεσθαι is the middle infinitive of θέρομαι ‘warm oneself’.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ Ὀδυσῆ’ ἐνένιπε Μελανθὼ δεύτερον αὖτις·
sentences.tr: hē d’ Odysē’ enenipe Melanthō deuteron autis·
sentences.l: And she Odysseus rebuked, Melantho, a second time, again:
sentences.i: Then Melantho rebuked Odysseus a second time:
sentences.n: Melantho is the maid who abused Odysseus at 18.321–336. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, and the name Μελανθώ comes after the verb. ἐνένιπε is ‘rebuked’, the aorist of ἐνίπτω. δεύτερον αὖτις is ‘a second time, again’, the two adverbs together stressing the repetition.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐνθάδ’ ἀνιήσεις διὰ νύκτα
δινεύων κατὰ οἶκον, ὀπιπεύσεις δὲ γυναῖκας;
sentences.tr:
xein’, eti kai nyn enthad’ aniēseis dia nykta
dineuōn kata oikon, opipeuseis de gynaikas;
sentences.l:
“Stranger, still even now here will you distress through the night,
roaming about the house, and will you spy on the women?
sentences.i: “Stranger, will you go on causing distress here even now, through the night, roaming about the house and spying on the women?
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε ‘stranger’, elided. ἔτι καὶ νῦν is ‘still, even now’. ἀνιήσεις is the future of ἀνιάω ‘distress, be a nuisance’, with no object given, and διὰ νύκτα is ‘through the night’. δινεύων is ‘roaming’, from δινεύω ‘whirl, go round and round’, and ὀπιπεύσεις is the future of ὀπιπεύω ‘look at, spy on’. The ; is the Greek question mark, and δέ adds a second verb to the same question.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔξελθε θύραζε, τάλαν, καὶ δαιτὸς ὄνησο·
sentences.tr: all’ exelthe thyraze, talan, kai daitos onēso·
sentences.l: But go out of doors, sorry soul, and have enjoyment of your meal;
sentences.i: But go out of doors, you sorry creature, and have your enjoyment of the meal;
sentences.n: τάλαν is the vocative of τάλας ‘wretched, suffering’, the word Melantho used to him at 18.327. ἔξελθε is the aorist imperative of ἐξέρχομαι ‘go out’, and θύραζε is ‘out of doors’, with the suffix -ζε ‘towards’. ὄνησο is the aorist imperative middle of ὀνίνημι ‘have profit or enjoyment of’, with the genitive δαιτός ‘meal’: a sneer, since he has had his food and should now go.

sentences.t: ἢ τάχα καὶ δαλῷ βεβλημένος εἶσθα θύραζε.
sentences.tr: ē tacha kai dalōi beblēmenos eistha thyraze.
sentences.l: or soon even by a firebrand struck you will go out of doors.”
sentences.i: or soon you will go out of doors struck by a firebrand.”
sentences.n: ἢ τάχα is ‘or soon’. δαλῷ βεβλημένος is ‘struck by a firebrand’: βεβλημένος is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω, and δαλός a burning stick. εἶσθα is the second singular of εἶμι ‘go’, here with future sense, ‘you will go’. θύραζε repeats the word of line 68, so that the threat echoes the order. Melantho’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at her with a scowl, spoke to her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς is a reply-formula with a look in it: ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking from under (the brows)’, a scowl, though the derivation of ὑπόδρα is not certain. πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is his stock epithet, translated every time. Murray begins a paragraph here.

sentences.t: δαιμονίη, τί μοι ὧδ’ ἐπέχεις κεκοτηότι θυμῷ;
sentences.tr: daimoniē, ti moi hōd’ epecheis kekotēoti thymōi;
sentences.l: “Strange woman, why to me thus do you press on, with a grudge-bearing heart?
sentences.i: “Strange woman, why do you bear down on me so, with a heart full of resentment?
sentences.n: δαιμονίη is the feminine of δαιμόνιος, an address whose force is uncertain, ‘strange one’; it seems to be said to someone whose behaviour puzzles the speaker. τί is ‘why’, ὧδ’ ‘so’, and ἐπέχεις is from ἐπέχω ‘hold, press upon’, here ‘press hard’ on someone. κεκοτηότι θυμῷ is a dative, ‘with a heart that bears a grudge’: κεκοτηότι is the perfect participle of κοτέω, from the same root as κότος ‘resentment’.

sentences.t:
ἦ ὅτι δὴ ῥυπόω, κακὰ δὲ χροῒ εἵματα εἷμαι,
πτωχεύω δ’ ἀνὰ δῆμον;
sentences.tr:
ē hoti dē rhypoō, kaka de chroï heimata heimai,
ptōcheuō d’ ana dēmon;
sentences.l:
Is it because indeed I am filthy, and evil clothes on my skin I wear,
and I beg throughout the land?
sentences.i: Is it because I am dirty, and wear vile clothes on my body, and beg throughout the land?
sentences.n: ἦ ὅτι δή is ‘is it because indeed’. ῥυπόω is ‘I am filthy’, an uncontracted present (Attic would contract it to ῥυπῶ). κακὰ … εἵματα εἷμαι is ‘I wear evil clothes’: εἷμαι is the perfect middle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’, with the clothes as object, and χροΐ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. πτωχεύω is ‘I beg’, and ἀνὰ δῆμον ‘throughout the land’. The ; is the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: ἀναγκαίη γὰρ ἐπείγει.
sentences.tr: anankaiē gar epeigei.
sentences.l: For necessity presses.
sentences.i: For necessity presses me.
sentences.n: ἀναγκαίη is ‘necessity’, and ἐπείγει ‘presses, drives’; γάρ gives the reason for the begging just mentioned. Odysseus says he begs because he must, not because he chooses to, and so answers Melantho’s sneer.

sentences.t:
τοιοῦτοι πτωχοὶ καὶ ἀλήμονες ἄνδρες ἔασι
καὶ γὰρ ἐγώ ποτε οἶκον ἐν ἀνθρώποισιν ἔναιον
ὄλβιος ἀφνειὸν καὶ πολλάκι δόσκον ἀλήτῃ,
τοίῳ ὁποῖος ἔοι καὶ ὅτευ κεχρημένος ἔλθοι·
sentences.tr:
toioutoi ptōchoi kai alēmones andres easi
kai gar egō pote oikon en anthrōpoisin enaion
olbios aphneion kai pollaki doskon alētēi,
toiōi hopoios eoi kai hoteu kechrēmenos elthoi·
sentences.i: Such are beggars and vagrants; for I too once lived among men in a rich house, a prosperous man, and I often used to give to a vagrant, to any man, whatever he might be and whatever he might come in need of;
sentences.n: He speaks as the disguised beggar, and the rich man who once gave to beggars is the past he gives himself. τοιοῦτοι ‘such’ points back to the dirt and begging; ἔασι is the Epic third plural of εἰμί (Attic εἰσί). No stop is printed after it, so the thought runs on into the next lines. Lines 75–77 are also 17.419–421, which he said to Antinous. ἔναιον is the imperfect of ναίω ‘inhabit’; ὄλβιος ‘prosperous’ describes the man, and ἀφνειόν ‘rich’ the house. δόσκον is an iterative imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘used to give’, with the suffix -σκ-. τοίῳ ὁποῖος ἔοι is ‘to one of whatever kind he might be’, and ὅτευ is ὅτου ‘of whatever’; κεχρημένος ‘in need of’ takes the genitive.

sentences.t:
ἦσαν δὲ δμῶες μάλα μυρίοι, ἄλλα τε πολλὰ
οἷσίν τ’ εὖ ζώουσι καὶ ἀφνειοὶ καλέονται.
sentences.tr:
ēsan de dmōes mala myrioi, alla te polla
hoisin t’ eu zōousi kai aphneioi kaleontai.
sentences.l:
And there were servants, very countless, and many other things
by which they live well and are called rich.
sentences.i: There were servants without number, and many other things by which people live well and are called rich.
sentences.n: δμῶες are ‘servants’, and μάλα μυρίοι is ‘very countless’. ἄλλα τε πολλά is ‘and many other things’, other possessions. οἷσίν τ’ is the dative relative ‘by which’, and ζώουσι is ζῶσι ‘they live’, with ‘people’ understood as subject. καλέονται is the uncontracted καλοῦνται ‘are called’. The same two lines stand at 17.422–423.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς ἀλάπαξε Κρονίων·
sentences.tr: alla Zeus alapaxe Kroniōn·
sentences.l: But Zeus, Cronus’ son, laid waste;
sentences.i: But Zeus, the son of Cronus, brought ruin;
sentences.n: ἀλάπαξε is the aorist of ἀλαπάζω ‘sack, lay waste’, and no object is given: the loss of his fortune is meant. Κρονίων is a patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’, here an epithet of Zeus.

sentences.t: ἤθελε γάρ που·
sentences.tr: ēthele gar pou·
sentences.l: for he wished it, I suppose;
sentences.i: it was his wish, I suppose;
sentences.n: ἤθελε is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’, and γάρ gives the reason. που is ‘I suppose’, a softening word: a man cannot know what a god intended.

sentences.t:
τῷ νῦν μήποτε καὶ σύ, γύναι, ἀπὸ πᾶσαν ὀλέσσῃς
ἀγλαΐην, τῇ νῦν γε μετὰ δμῳῇσι κέκασσαι·
sentences.tr:
tōi nyn mēpote kai sy, gynai, apo pasan olessēis
aglaïēn, tēi nyn ge meta dmōiēisi kekassai·
sentences.l:
therefore now never you too, woman, lose all
splendour, by which now at least among the maidservants you excel;
sentences.i: So now do not you too, woman, ever lose all the beauty by which you now stand out among the maids;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘therefore’. μήποτε with the aorist subjunctive ὀλέσσῃς is a warning, ‘never lose’, and ἀπὸ … ὀλέσσῃς is a tmesis of ἀπολέσῃς, with the double σ of Epic verse. γύναι is ‘woman’, the plain address. ἀγλαΐην is ‘splendour’, her beauty and standing. τῇ is the dative relative ‘by which’, and κέκασσαι is the perfect middle of καίνυμαι ‘excel’, second singular. μετὰ δμῳῇσι is ‘among the maidservants’.

sentences.t:
μή πώς τοι δέσποινα κοτεσσαμένη χαλεπήνῃ,
ἢ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔλθῃ·
sentences.tr:
mē pōs toi despoina kotessamenē chalepēnēi,
ē Odyseus elthēi·
sentences.l:
lest somehow your mistress, bearing a grudge, be harsh with you,
or Odysseus come;
sentences.i: for fear that your mistress, bearing a grudge, may deal harshly with you, or that Odysseus may come;
sentences.n: μή πώς τοι with the subjunctive χαλεπήνῃ is a fear, ‘lest somehow … she be harsh with you’, and ἢ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔλθῃ is a second fear under the same μή. δέσποινα is the ‘mistress’, Penelope. κοτεσσαμένη is ‘bearing a grudge’, the aorist participle of κοτέω, and χαλεπήνῃ is from χαλεπαίνω ‘be harsh, be angry’. Odysseus warns the maid about the return of a man who is standing in front of her.

sentences.t: ἔτι γὰρ καὶ ἐλπίδος αἶσα.
sentences.tr: eti gar kai elpidos aisa.
sentences.l: for there is still even of hope a portion.
sentences.i: for there is still some portion of hope.
sentences.n: Odysseus, still disguised, speaks of Odysseus in the third person, and the audience knows he is in the hall. αἶσα is ‘portion, allotted share’, from the same root as αἴσιμα ‘in due measure’, and ἐλπίδος is ‘of hope’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ὁ μὲν ὣς ἀπόλωλε καὶ οὐκέτι νόστιμός ἐστιν,
ἀλλ’ ἤδη παῖς τοῖος Ἀπόλλωνός γε ἕκητι,
Τηλέμαχος·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ ho men hōs apolōle kai ouketi nostimos estin,
all’ ēdē pais toios Apollōnos ge hekēti,
Tēlemachos·
sentences.i: But if he has perished in that way and is not coming home any more, there is already such a son, by Apollo’s will — Telemachus;
sentences.n: ἀπόλωλε is the perfect of ἀπόλλυμι ‘has perished’, and ὣς is ‘so, in that way’. νόστιμος is ‘one who will come home’, formed from νόστος ‘homecoming’. ἀλλά begins the answer, ‘yet’. τοῖος is ‘such’, and the name of the son is held back to the first word of line 87. Ἀπόλλωνός γε ἕκητι is ‘by the will of Apollo’: ἕκητι with a genitive is ‘by the will of’, the opposite of ἀέκητι ‘against the will of’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὔ τις ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναικῶν
λήθει ἀτασθάλλουσ’, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι τηλίκος ἐστίν.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ou tis eni megaroisi gynaikōn
lēthei atasthallous’, epei ouketi tēlikos estin.
sentences.l:
and him no one of the women in the halls
escapes, acting wantonly, since no longer so young is he.”
sentences.i: and no woman in the halls who acts wantonly escapes his notice, since he is no longer so young.”
sentences.n: λήθει is λανθάνει ‘escapes the notice of’, with the accusative τόν ‘him’. οὔ τις … γυναικῶν is ‘none of the women’, a partitive genitive. ἀτασθάλλουσ’ is the participle of ἀτασθάλλω ‘act wantonly’, from the root of ἀτασθαλίαι ‘wanton follies’ at 1.7. τηλίκος is ‘of such an age’, and with οὐκέτι the sense is ‘no longer so young’. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοῦ δ’ ἤκουσε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
ἀμφίπολον δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tou d’ ēkouse periphrōn Pēnelopeia,
amphipolon d’ enenipen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and him heard circumspect Penelope,
and her attendant she rebuked and spoke a word and called her by name:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and circumspect Penelope heard him, and she rebuked her attendant, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. τοῦ δ’ ἤκουσε is ‘and she heard him’: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard. ἀμφίπολον is ‘attendant’, Melantho. ἐνένιπεν is ‘rebuked’. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is the formula ‘and spoke a word and called by name’, with ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε a tmesis; Penelope in fact does not name Melantho, and the formula only says she spoke to her directly.

sentences.t:
πάντως, θαρσαλέη, κύον ἀδεές, οὔ τί με λήθεις
ἔρδουσα μέγα ἔργον, ὃ σῇ κεφαλῇ ἀναμάξεις·
sentences.tr:
pantōs, tharsaleē, kyon adees, ou ti me lētheis
erdousa mega ergon, ho sēi kephalēi anamaxeis·
sentences.l:
“Altogether, bold one, unafraid dog, not at all me you escape
doing a great deed, which on your own head you will wipe off;
sentences.i: “Certainly, you bold one, you unafraid dog, you do not escape my notice when you do a great deed, which you will wipe off on your own head;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here, and Penelope turns on Melantho. πάντως is ‘certainly’. θαρσαλέη is a feminine vocative ‘bold one’. κύον ἀδεές is ‘unafraid dog’: ‘dog’ is an insult, and ἀδεές is ‘fearless, shameless’ (ἀ- + δέος ‘fear’). οὔ τί με λήθεις is ‘you do not escape my notice’, and ἔρδουσα is ‘doing’. ὃ σῇ κεφαλῇ ἀναμάξεις is ‘which you will wipe off on your own head’: ἀναμάσσω is ‘wipe off’, and the guilt is pictured as a stain wiped onto the head of the one who bears it, so she will answer for the deed herself.

sentences.t:
πάντα γὰρ εὖ ᾔδησθ’, ἐπεὶ ἐξ ἐμεῦ ἔκλυες αὐτῆς
ὡς τὸν ξεῖνον ἔμελλον ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἐμοῖσιν
ἀμφὶ πόσει εἴρεσθαι, ἐπεὶ πυκινῶς ἀκάχημαι.
sentences.tr:
panta gar eu ēidēsth’, epei ex emeu eklyes autēs
hōs ton xeinon emellon eni megaroisin emoisin
amphi posei eiresthai, epei pykinōs akachēmai.
sentences.l:
for all things well you knew, since from me myself you heard
how the stranger I was going, in my halls,
about my husband to ask, since closely I am grieved.”
sentences.i: for you knew it all well, since you heard from me myself that I meant to question the stranger in my halls about my husband, because I am heavily grieved.”
sentences.n: ᾔδησθ’ is ᾔδησθα, the second singular pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘you knew’. ἔκλυες is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, and ἐξ ἐμεῦ … αὐτῆς is ‘from me myself’, ἐμεῦ being Ionic ἐμοῦ. ὡς with ἔμελλον and the infinitive εἴρεσθαι is ‘that I was going to ask’, εἴρεσθαι being the present infinitive of εἴρομαι. ἀμφὶ πόσει is ‘about my husband’, ἀμφί with the dative of πόσις. πυκινῶς is ‘closely, thickly’, so ‘deeply’, and ἀκάχημαι is the perfect of ἀχέω ‘grieve’, ‘I am grieved’. Penelope’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥα καὶ Εὐρυνόμην ταμίην πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: ē rha kai Eurynomēn tamiēn pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l: She spoke, and Eurynome the housekeeper with a word addressed:
sentences.i: So she said, and spoke to the housekeeper Eurynome:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. ἦ ῥα καί is ‘she spoke, and’: ἦ is from ἠμί ‘say’. Εὐρυνόμην ταμίην is ‘Eurynome the housekeeper’, in the accusative. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is a tmesis of προσεῖπεν ‘addressed’, with μῦθον ‘with a word’. ταμίη is the housekeeper in charge of the stores.

sentences.t:
Εὐρυνόμη, φέρε δὴ δίφρον καὶ κῶας ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ,
ὄφρα καθεζόμενος εἴπῃ ἔπος ἠδ’ ἐπακούσῃ
ὁ ξεῖνος ἐμέθεν·
sentences.tr:
Eurynomē, phere dē diphron kai kōas ep’ autou,
ophra kathezomenos eipēi epos ēd’ epakousēi
ho xeinos emethen·
sentences.i: “Eurynome, come now, bring a stool and a fleece on it, so that the stranger may sit down and speak, and listen to me;
sentences.n: φέρε δή is ‘come now, bring’, the imperative of φέρω. δίφρος is a ‘stool’, and κῶας a ‘fleece’; ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ is ‘on it’. ὄφρα with the subjunctives εἴπῃ and ἐπακούσῃ is ‘so that he may say … and listen’. καθεζόμενος is ‘sitting down’. ἐπακούσῃ takes the genitive ἐμέθεν, the Epic form of ἐμοῦ ‘me’, ‘listen to me’. The subject, ὁ ξεῖνος ‘the stranger’, is held back to the start of line 99.

sentences.t: ἐθέλω δέ μιν ἐξερέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: ethelō de min exereesthai.
sentences.l: and I wish to question him.”
sentences.i: for I want to question him.”
sentences.n: ἐθέλω is ‘I wish’, and ἐξερέεσθαι is the infinitive of ἐξερέομαι ‘question closely’; μιν is ‘him’, the stranger. Penelope’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡ δὲ μάλ’ ὀτραλέως κατέθηκε φέρουσα
δίφρον ἐΰξεστον καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ κῶας ἔβαλλεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hē de mal’ otraleōs katethēke pherousa
diphron eÿxeston kai ep’ autōi kōas eballen·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and she then very briskly put down, bringing it,
a well-polished stool and on it a fleece she threw;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the housekeeper very promptly brought a well-polished stool and put it down, and threw a fleece on it;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ὣς ἔφατο ‘So she spoke’, and ἡ δέ is ‘and she’, Eurynome. ὀτραλέως is ‘promptly, briskly’. κατέθηκε φέρουσα is ‘put down, bringing’: the participle gives the first action. ἐΰξεστον is ‘well-polished’, from ἐύ- ‘well’ and ξεστός ‘polished, planed’, and δίφρον is ‘stool’. ἔβαλλεν is the imperfect, ‘she threw’, with ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘on it’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἔπειτα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr: entha kathezet’ epeita polytlas dios Odysseus.
sentences.l: There then sat down much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: There much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus sat down.
sentences.n: ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἔπειτα is the formula of line 59, now of Odysseus: both are seated. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς gives him two stock epithets, ‘much-enduring’ and ‘heavenly’, translated every time.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Circumspect Penelope was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε is the formula ‘and among them she began the speeches’, ‘was the first to speak among them’: ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘begin’, with the genitive μύθων. It stands at 17.100, of Penelope too. Her speech to Odysseus follows this line.
